The getter is now defined to return the *current* ATT_MTU at read time, so a fresh read always reflects the present value; the maxwritewithoutresponsesizechanged event is just a convenience notification fired when the UA observes a change, not the only way the value updates.

That lines up with the Chromium CL: the value is seeded from the live MTU at characteristic enumeration and refreshed by the event on BlueZ/Android/WinRT. its not 100% "fresh" but the caching is what i think implementational detail, as the developer observed value always represents the real value.

macOS is the one platform with no MTU-change callback, but CoreBluetooth settles the ATT_MTU at connection time (before characteristics are discovered) and never renegotiates, so the value there is final from the first read and never goes stale.

body:
If the platform will change its answer without firing an event and the browser is caching the value then it doesn't matter if the platform silently changes it because the browser won't notice. I think this is fine, and if the browser does check again for some reason then it could fire an event and update the value.

The key thing is that unless we go back to the asynchronous `getMTU()` method, we can't guarantee that the attribute will reflect the latest value _unless_ the OS provides an event. At best, when the site accesses the attribute we could trigger a check in the background and fire an event if we discover a new value.

body:
I would expect the implementation to either not cache the value if a synchronous getter is available on the OS. Or cache the value and always be subscribed to changes if there isn't such a getter.

In other words, I would expect reading the `maxWriteWithoutResponseSize` attribute in the browser would synchronously call `GattSession.MaxPduSize` on WinRT and `maximumWriteValueLengthForType(CBCharacteristicWriteWithoutResponse)` on CoreBluetooth.

For BlueZ, I would expect that we are already subscribed to D-Bus property changes on characteristics so should always have the latest value without having to do an async D-Bus call. Similarly, on Android, I would expect that we would always be subscribed to `onMtuChanged` so that we always have the latest value available.

I don't think I have anything else to add to the discussion at this point (I'm just an interested 3rd party, so any final decisions are not up to me. :smile:).

OK, maybe one thing...

The trouble with trying to block on Windows until there is a MTU event is that the event may never come, e.g. if a device only supports minimum MTU. And there isn't a way to know this in advance. And there is no universal upper bound on how long it will take for the event to come. We tried doing something like this in Bleak and quickly reverted it because it didn't work well in practice.

Since the event should come relatively quickly after connect, our solution was to just poll the property until it changed from the default (and only on devices/characteristics that actually need it).

```python
            async with asyncio.timeout(10):
                while char.max_write_without_response_size == 20:
                    await asyncio.sleep(0.5)
```

This still works without wasting any time on non-Windows platforms too (and avoids the issue with macOS not having an event). The JavaScript equivalent won't be as elegant, but should still work just fine.

Sorry for letting this stagnate for a while. I had other tasks to focus on.

Helmut's example in https://github.com/WebBluetoothCG/web-bluetooth/pull/672#discussion_r3501845691 is exactly the type of code I would expect developers to write and if implementations keep `maxWriteWithoutResponseSize` up to date when they notice a change then it seems like that will be good enough for most use cases. We can still provide a `maxwritewithoutresponsesizechanged` event, but it would only be useful in cases where a developer might've prechunked the data for some reason and want to consider rechunking it.

The key assumption that I think makes this work is that it is okay for the `maxWriteWithoutResponseSize` value the site is using to be out-of-date as it will only increase during a connection. If it ever decreased then I think writes would start failing (or being truncated) which would be a problem.
